# wf-router — knowledge-base router

A thin router, not a knowledge source. It tells you **which** `lang-*` / `hw-*` skill to open for a given
language + architecture, and the **discipline** for reading it. It holds no APIs, schemas, or hardware
capability/spec tables — those belong to each `hw-*` skill's `specs.md`, `cudagym`, and `kernel-factory-schemas`.
(It *does* map product names / `sm_XX` codes to the right skill — that is routing; see §1.2.)

**Where this sits:** run `query` first (it fetches the problem and the `target_hardware` from
`strategy_config`/env + `/problem/`). Then use this router to choose what to read. `wf-kernelgen` (design /
write) and `wf-optimize` (improve) invoke this at their KB-reading step. Evaluation goes through `cudagym`;
learnings go through `insights`. This skill never runs a kernel or writes a trace log.

> All skill paths below are rooted at `$SOLSWARM_SKILLS_DIR/<skill-name>`. The KB skills are the rebuilt
> `lang-*` (language) and `hw-*` (hardware) skills — there are no `*-expert` skills.

## 1. Routing tables

### Language → `lang-*` skill

Pick the language skill from what the kernel is (or will be) written in.

| Context clue | Language skill | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `import cutlass.cute as cute`, `@cute.jit`, `@cute.kernel`, `from_dlpack`, tcgen05 | **`lang-cutedsl`** | **Generation target.** Tiered — see §1.1. |
| `@cute.experimental.kernel` / `cute_ext.*`, `lir.dot`, `lir.tma_load`, explicit pipeline classes | **`lang-lir`** | **Generation target. Blackwell only: SM100/SM103 (B200/B300) + SM120 (GB202 / RTX PRO 6000)** — see §1.3. Flat numbered chapters + `index.md`. |
| `import cutlass.experimental.primitives as prims`, `prims.*` raw ops, `cutlass.Array`, hand-built MMA descriptors | **`lang-cutedsl`** — CTM chapters | **Generation target.** CTM is a *second authoring model inside* CuTe DSL, so it routes to the same skill, not a separate one: read `core/` ch20–27, plus `sm100/` ch22–25 or `sm120/` ch22 for the arch half. **Blackwell only** (same gate as LIR) — see §1.3. |
| `.cu` / `.cuh`, WGMMA / Gen5 / `tcgen05.mma` intrinsics, TMA descriptors, inline PTX | **`lang-cuda-c-ptx`** | **Generation target.** Has a `## Workflows` section + per-path `*_verification_checklist.md` / `*_common_pitfalls.md` — start from those. Read the core/base instructions before the specialized (gen5/bmm/group-gemm) ones — the specialized docs assume the base set. |
| `import cuda.tile as ct`, `@ct.kernel`, `ct.launch`, `ct.mma` | **`lang-cutile`** | **Generation target.** Flat files + `index.md`. |
| PTX ISA instruction lookup, operand/encoding semantics (NOT authoring a whole kernel) | **`lang-ptx-reference`** | **Reference only** — never a generation target. Supplement to the above when debugging emitted PTX. |
| MLIR / CuTe-dialect ops, lowering pipeline, `cutlass-opt`, compiler-IR analysis | **`lang-cutlass-ir`** | **Analysis only** — never a generation target. |

### Architecture → `hw-*` skill (supplement, DSL-agnostic)

Add the matching hardware skill when the task touches microarchitecture, memory hierarchy, MMA path, or
tuning. The target GPU comes from `cudagym` / the `solution.json` `target_hardware` — do not restate that
mapping here.

| Target family | Hardware skill | Add when |
|---|---|---|
| Hopper (H100/H200) | **`hw-hopper`** | WGMMA path, warpgroup occupancy, Hopper TMA/pipeline tuning |
| Blackwell (B200/B300) | **`hw-blackwell`** | tcgen05/UMMA, TMEM, 2-CTA MMA, GEMM tuning; has `specs.md`, concise tuning chapters, and source-faithful compatibility/SM/GB200/Grace/OS/training/microbenchmark references |
| Rubin (R100) | **`hw-rubin`** | Rubin deltas — doubled-K MMA, LUT-B, Lamport sync, 576-col TMEM, softmax accel; has `specs.md` |
| GeForce / RTX PRO 6000 (GB202) | **`hw-blackwell-geforce`** | SM120 warp-synchronous `mma.sync` path (NOT tcgen05) |

### 1.1 `lang-cutedsl` is tiered — read core + the target tier

`lang-cutedsl/references/` is organized **by architecture tier**, each tier with its own `index.md` and
`known_limitations.md`. Always read `core/` plus the one tier for your target. Do **not** read every tier.

| Target | Tiers to open (`references/<tier>/`) | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Hopper | `core/` + `sm90/` | `examples/hopper/` |
| Blackwell | `core/` + `sm100/` (+ `optimization/` when tuning) | `examples/blackwell/` |
| GeForce GB202 | `core/` + `sm120/` (**standalone** — do NOT read `sm100`; APIs differ) | `examples/blackwell_geforce/` |

> Examples keep DKG's architecture folder names (not `smXXX`); shared utilities live in `examples/helpers/`.

The SM100 optimization playbook (`optimization/`) is dual-DSL (CuTe + LIR) and is cross-referenced from the
`sm100/` chapters; reach for it from `wf-optimize`, not on first read.

### 1.2 Product / chip / SM → which skill

Resolve a product name or `sm_XX` code to the right tier/skill (and recognize variants the harness may name).
A variant with no dedicated skill falls back to its closest covered base.

| Product / name | Chip | CUDA SM | Knowledge skills |
|---|---|---|---|

| Blackwell B200 | GB100 | `sm_100a` | `hw-blackwell` + `lang-cutedsl/sm100` (+ `lang-lir`) |
| Blackwell B300 ("Carrot") | GB110 | `sm_103a/f` | `hw-blackwell` (SM103 = B300 variant) + `lang-cutedsl/sm100` (+ `lang-lir`) |
| Rubin R100 | GR100 | `sm_107a/f` | `hw-rubin` only — **no CuTe DSL tier** (see §1.3) |
| GeForce / RTX PRO 6000 (GB202) | GB20(2/3) | `sm_120a` | `hw-blackwell-geforce` + `lang-cutedsl/sm120` (+ `lang-lir`) |
| Thor (Blackwell iGPU) | GB10B | `sm_110a/f` | *no dedicated skill* — closest base `hw-blackwell` / `lang-cutedsl/sm100` |
| Rubin GR150 | GR150 | `sm_109a/f` | *no dedicated skill* — closest base `hw-rubin` |
| ADA-Next Tegra | GB20B | `sm_121a` | *no dedicated skill* — closest `hw-blackwell-geforce` / `lang-cutedsl/sm120` |
| Rubin-Next (iGPU) | GR20x | `sm_124a` | *future — not covered* |

This is a routing aid, not capability data: the actual per-target hardware numbers live in each `hw-*`
skill's `specs.md` and in `cudagym` / `kernel-factory-schemas`.

### 1.3 Routing facts (high-signal, do not relearn)

- **LIR and CTM are Blackwell-only: SM100/SM103 (B200/B300) and SM120/SM121 (GB202 / RTX PRO 6000,
  GB10).** If the target is not one of those, do not route to `lang-lir` or to the CTM chapters; use
  plain `lang-cutedsl` instead. Kernel Factory enforces this at campaign create — a `lir` or `ctm`
  campaign on non-Blackwell hardware is rejected with a `400` before any GPU time is spent. CTM has no
  `sm90` chapters at all, so there is nothing to read for it on Hopper.
- **Rubin (SM107) has no CuTe DSL tier in this iteration.** The `sm107` tier and `examples/rubin/` were
  removed for the CUTLASS 4.7 KB refresh and will return later. Rubin hardware and ISA knowledge is
  unaffected — route to `hw-rubin` (and `lang-ptx-reference/references/rubin-ptx/` for PTX). For DSL
  authoring, read `core/` + `sm100/` as the closest foundation, but treat SM107-specific behaviour
  (doubled K, LUT-B, Lamport sync, TMA override + valid-check, 576-col TMEM) as **undocumented here** —
  `hw-rubin` is the authority. Do NOT treat R100 as "just Blackwell with more SMs."
- **CuTe is NOT missing the big instructions — do not route to CTM to reach one.** Every large hardware
  instruction already exists as a CuTe *atom*: tcgen05 (`cute.nvgpu.tcgen05`), WGMMA
  (`cute.nvgpu.warpgroup`), `ldmatrix`/`stmatrix` (`cute.nvgpu.warp`), and TMA incl. im2col and multicast
  (`cute.nvgpu.cpasync`). What differs between CuTe and CTM is the layer *above* the instruction, not the
  instruction. Route to CTM for a raw PTX field an atom fixes by policy, or for a deliberate whole-kernel
  CTM design — never because "CuTe can't do tcgen05".
- **CTM carries no layout algebra, and that is the cost.** Nothing in `prims.*` does partitioning,
  division, composition or coalescing. Whole-kernel CTM means hand-deriving the descriptor constants
  layout algebra would otherwise derive — once per tile shape, dtype and swizzle. Recommend it only for a
  fixed shape and dtype whose constants can be pinned. CTM also has no kernel decorator: entry is always
  `@cute.kernel` / `@cute.jit`, so a CTM kernel is *expected* to contain `cute.*`.
- **SM120 (GeForce GB202) is NOT tcgen05 and is standalone.** It uses warp-synchronous
  `mma.sync.aligned.kind::*`, not `tcgen05.mma`/TMEM/UMMA. Do not transplant an SM100 kernel onto SM120 —
  use the SM120-native chapters of the chosen language instead: `lang-cutedsl` `sm120/` for CuTe DSL,
  `lang-lir` SM120 chapters (`13_sm120_target.md` + `22_example_sm120_pingpong.md`) for LIR, plus
  `hw-blackwell-geforce` for hardware specs.

## 2. Reading discipline

Apply to every KB skill. The goal is to pull only what the current problem needs, verbatim, into context.
Let the current context drive what you pull — the source kernel (if porting/optimizing), the exact
compiler/runtime error (if fixing), and the user's request define what "relevant" means.

1. **Open the skill's index, not a hardcoded chapter name.** Each KB skill's `SKILL.md` (and, for tiered/
   per-tier layouts, each `references/<tier>/index.md`) is itself a keyword→file routing table — scan it for
   the term closest to your task and let it name the exact reference file(s) to open. Do not guess
   filenames; chapter numbering varies by skill and changes over time.
2. **Read `known_limitations.md` first** (in `lang-cutedsl` it is per-tier; `lang-lir` and `lang-cutile`
   carry one — `lang-cutile` names it `known_issues.md`). These are short, high-signal, and prevent
   rediscovering documented issues mid-implementation. For `lang-cuda-c-ptx`, the equivalent entry points
   are its `## Workflows` section plus the per-path `*_verification_checklist.md` / `*_common_pitfalls.md`.
3. **Read 2–4 relevant chapters, NOT all of them.** Pull the quickstart/overview for the language and the
   chapter for the canonical pattern closest to the task (e.g. a dense-GEMM tutorial for a GEMM, an FMHA
   chapter for attention). Reading an entire doc tree upfront burns the context budget and has caused
   session failures on complex kernels. Read more chapters on-demand when the work hits a specific gap.
   **Process one file at a time** — read it, pull only the sections that bear on the current problem, then
   move to the next. Do not open many files at once and interleave them.
   - When a KB skill ships runnable examples (e.g. `lang-cutedsl` `examples/<tier>/`), pull the closest one
     as a starting template — examples serve generation, repair, porting, and optimization, not just
     debugging.
4. **Grep before opening.** Search `references/` for the exact concept first:
   ```bash
   grep -rn 'scale.*factor\|SFA\|SFB'   "$SOLSWARM_SKILLS_DIR/lang-cuda-c-ptx/references/"
   grep -rn 'Bkeep\|Breuse\|LUT-?B'      "$SOLSWARM_SKILLS_DIR/hw-rubin/references/"
   grep -rn '2-CTA\|two-CTA\|TMEM'       "$SOLSWARM_SKILLS_DIR/hw-blackwell/references/"
   grep -rn 'ct\.mma\|matmul'            "$SOLSWARM_SKILLS_DIR/lang-cutile/references/"
   ```
5. **Quote verbatim, do not paraphrase.** When you bring a section into context, copy the original text
   exactly — the docs are carefully authored. Paraphrasing API signatures, operand constraints, or
   tolerances silently drops load-bearing exactness. Do not summarize or rewrite, and do not dump whole
   files; take only the relevant sections.

# wf-validate — kernel rules + optional pre-eval lint

Two things in one place, both used by `wf-kernelgen` and `wf-optimize`:
- **Part A — the invariants** every kernel-generation / optimization task must follow (read once).
- **Part B — an optional structural lint** to sanity-check a kernel cheaply *before* a `cudagym` round.

---

## Part A — Shared invariants

### 1. Anti-cheat: the solution must be a real kernel

The submitted kernel must do the actual work **in the chosen DSL/language** (CuTe DSL, LIR, CUDA-C, or CuTile).

- **No framework/library call doing the computation** — `torch.matmul`, `torch.nn.functional.*`, cuBLAS, cuDNN, Triton, `np.*`, etc. must not stand in for the kernel. Host code may only set up inputs, launch the kernel, and collect outputs.
- A user-provided reference (PyTorch, pseudocode, another kernel) is **read-only** — use it to understand correctness, not as the implementation.
- `cudagym` enforces this server-side: a kernel that offloads the work is scored **`REWARD_HACK`**, and `submit`'s compliance judge independently rejects framework-kernel and cuda-graph cheats. There is no way to win by faking it — write the real kernel.

### 2. DPS `run()` contract

The kernel is exposed through a Destination-Passing-Style `run()` entrypoint. **Do not restate the schema here** — `kernel-factory-schemas` is the authority for the exact `run()` signature, `solution.json` / `definition.json` shape, and how outputs are written into caller-provided destination tensors. Read it (or `cudagym`'s references) when you need the precise contract; just remember the kernel must conform to it or `cudagym` will reject it before scoring.

### 3. Output & working hygiene

- **Rank changes by expected impact.** Lead with the highest-leverage change.
- **Edit incrementally.** `Write` the file once to create it, then `Edit` for every subsequent change — edit only the section that needs to change, don't rewrite the whole file. This avoids endless-rewrite loops.
- **Keep a concise results view.** Report what changed and the resulting `cudagym` Trace (status + correctness + latency/speedup) compactly; don't re-paste unchanged code or full logs.

### 4. Frozen-skill boundary

The action skills **orchestrate** the frozen harness; they never re-implement it:

- **Don't re-fetch / re-parse the problem** — it arrives via injected context; use **`query`**.
- **Don't re-implement the runner or scorer** (and don't restate `sm_XX`/`target_hardware` tables) — evaluate via **`cudagym`**.
- **Don't keep a private local learning or trace log** — consume candidate outcomes via **`insights`** (and consume the injected round summary from **`summarize`**).

---

## Part B — Optional structural lint (pre-`cudagym`)

A fast, **optional** structural lint — run it when a kernel is cheap to sanity-check before committing a `cudagym evaluate` round. **Never a mandatory gate**: `cudagym`'s `COMPILE_ERROR` / `INCORRECT_*` / `REWARD_HACK` statuses already cover wrong-DSL, broken structure, and cheating. This is a cheap heads-up, not a substitute.

**Use** it for freshly written/ported kernels, or when you suspect a framework shortcut or an unfinished stub. **Skip** it whenever you're already confident.

### What it checks

1. **Right DSL / entry point** for the chosen language (correct decorator, a real kernel entry).
2. **Anti-cheat** (Part A §1): no library silently doing the core computation; host code only sets up and launches.
3. **No empty/unwritten stub**: kernel body is non-trivial and outputs are actually written.
4. **Basic structural sanity**: valid syntax, required imports, signatures/dtypes/shapes look consistent.

It does **not** check correctness, layouts, barriers, or performance — that is `cudagym`'s job.

### How to run it

Spawn one lint subagent over the kernel source using the matching reference prompt. The subagent is **Read/Grep/Glob only** and its **fir…350 tokens truncated…examples for CUDA Tensor Core kernel development across WGMMA (Hopper) and Gen5/tcgen05 (Blackwell) architectures.

## When to Use

Use this skill when working with CUDA C tensor core kernels:
- Generating GEMM or BMM kernels with WGMMA (Hopper) or tcgen05.mma (Blackwell)
- Working with TMA tensor maps, shared memory descriptors, or instruction descriptors
- Implementing NVFP4/MXFP8 block-scaled kernels with E2M1 format

# Blackwell (SM100) Architecture & Optimization

Architectural reference and optimization guide for NVIDIA datacenter Blackwell GPUs (B200, B300) targeting SM100/SM103 compute capabilities. Covers 5th-generation tensor cores (tcgen05 MMA), Tensor Memory (TMEM), the full memory hierarchy, and Blackwell-specific kernel optimization.

> **Other Blackwell-family targets** are covered by separate sibling skills:
> - **Rubin (R100, SM107)** — delta on top of SM100 → `hw-rubin`
> - **Blackwell GeForce / RTX PRO 6000 (GB202, SM120)** — different MMA path (warp-synchronous `mma.sync.aligned.kind::*`, NOT tcgen05) → `hw-blackwell-geforce`

## When to Use

- Choosing between 1-CTA and 2-CTA MMA modes
- Managing TMEM allocation, lifecycle, and fencing
- Tuning pipeline depth and occupancy for latency hiding
- Diagnosing tensor-core, memory, or epilog bottlenecks on Blackwell
- Migrating Hopper kernels to Blackwell
- Checking application/binary compatibility for Blackwell
